paragraphs: The core deliverable of nanotechnology engineering technologists and technicians is operating nanoscale equipment per controlled procedures, preparing and testing samples, and leaving reviewable parameter and result records; the work is usually carried out under the supervision of nanotechnology engineering staff, and judging fit starts with real tasks and the equipment environment, not the job title.

Complete one small exercise using public equipment manuals or simulated parameters: write the operating steps, safety preconditions, record fields, and abnormal shutdown conditions, and then ask an experienced technician to give feedback against on-site standards.

Positive signals: willing to operate equipment per procedures over the long term, record parameters item by item, and accept repeated measurement and cleaning and maintenance; caution signals: hard to follow safety procedures and cleanliness requirements, avoiding record review, or expecting to do only design and not execution.

Paper exercises and simulated operation do not constitute equipment operation qualifications, cleanroom access, or safety permits; when nanoparticles, chemicals, radiation, or high-pressure equipment are involved, work must be carried out under the supervision of trained personnel according to employer and local rules.

Nanotechnology engineering technologists and technicians ({{fact:identity}}) implement production processes under the supervision of nanotechnology engineering staff, operating commercial-scale equipment to produce, test, or modify materials, devices, or systems with unique molecular or macromolecular composition, and use advanced microscopy equipment to manipulate nanoscale objects; the deliverables are reproducible process parameters, measurement data, and equipment records.

entries: Carry out production and preparation steps for nanomaterials or devices per work instructions.
Operate and maintain nanofabrication, coating, etching, or inspection equipment and record parameters.
Use equipment such as electron microscopes and atomic force microscopes to observe and manipulate nanoscale objects.
Measure samples by standard methods and organize the measurement data.
Perform testing and inspection on products, processes, or systems, and record deviations.
Calibrate equipment, replace consumables, and complete cleaning and maintenance.
Record data as required, write reports, and hand over to engineers or supervisors.
Follow safety, chemical, and cleanroom procedures, and shut down and report when something is abnormal.

paragraphs: O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone 4 (SVP 7.0 to less than 8.0): it requires extensive job-related skills, knowledge, or experience, usually several years of related work experience, on-the-job training, or vocational training; the interest code is {{fact:interest-code}}, indicating that the work is mainly equipment operation, measurement, and standardized record keeping.

The daily loop is usually: confirm the task and safety preconditions → prepare samples and equipment → operate per procedures and record parameters → measure and inspect → review anomalies and report → hand over data and equipment status. The whole process emphasizes traceability rather than delivering results only.

The working environment for nanotechnology engineering technologists and technicians is usually the manufacturing floor and the laboratory: the O*NET industry page shows this occupation distributed mainly across manufacturing (75%), professional scientific and technical services (11%), and other industries (14%), and equipment, cleanliness classes, and safety requirements differ considerably across settings.

The difference from adjacent positions lies in the scope of responsibility and decision authority: nanosystems engineers are responsible for design, plans, and result judgments, while this occupation executes operations, measurements, and maintenance per the plan; manufacturing technicians focus on general production line equipment, while this occupation centers on nanoscale equipment and samples.

Software or equipment mentioned in job postings (such as data analysis, imaging software, office software, and microscopy equipment) only indicate the work environment and technology preferences; they do not prove that all positions require these tools, nor that automation has been achieved.

Capability evidence for operating positions comes from reviewable records: equipment parameter records, sample measurement data, calibration and maintenance records, and abnormal shutdown and handling records; these records also determine that responsibility boundaries can be traced clearly.

The biggest difference between nanotechnology engineering technologists and technicians and adjacent occupations is the scope of responsibility: this occupation executes equipment operation, measurement, and maintenance per an established plan, while design and result judgments are borne by engineers.

The comparison basis is each occupation's official task descriptions and employer responsibility statements; the same job title may correspond to different task combinations in different organizations, and this page only makes directional distinctions and does not represent mutual recognition of qualifications.

The table below compares this occupation with adjacent directions by main object, core output, and authorization boundary, to help judge which real tasks to look at rather than choosing by title similarity.

It takes the operation of nanoscale equipment, sample preparation, and measurement as its core object and delivers traceable parameters and measurement records; nanosystems engineers deliver design plans and result judgments as their core output.

If you would rather operate equipment per procedures, prepare samples, and do repeated measurements, compare this occupation; if you care more about plan design, technical roadmaps, and result interpretation, compare nanosystems engineers.

Students and career changers: first complete one operation and recording exercise using public manuals or simulated data, confirm whether you are willing to execute per procedures and repeat measurements over the long term, and only then discuss tool speed-up.
Use tools for materials retrieval, parameter organizing, and drafting records; equipment operation, sample handling, and safety shutdown judgments must be done by trained personnel.
Equipment operation and preparation positions: tools may help organize equipment logs and process parameters, while equipment status judgments and anomaly handling remain your responsibility.

Do not submit undisclosed formulations, process parameters, or client sample information to unauthorized services; measurement data must be checked back against the original records and equipment logs.
Inspection and measurement positions: tools may help with data organizing and image processing, while acceptance criteria and release conclusions are still confirmed by authorized people.
Responsibility does not change because of tools: equipment safety, cleanliness procedures, and result release responsibility remain with trained personnel and the employer.

On-site supervisors and equipment owners: specify which tools may be used, the scope of data that may be processed, and the record-keeping requirements, and state the situations that require shutdown and reporting.

Read employment evidence separately: the O*NET wages and employment use the Industrial Engineering Technologists and Technicians parent occupation scope, and the page has not published generative AI adoption rates or job change data for this occupation, so they cannot be pieced together into a replacement conclusion.

Insufficient evidence: no national occupational wage median under the same scope as O*NET 17-3026.01 was obtained in this round; the National Bureau of Statistics industry annual average wages that were verified can only serve as an industry reference, and it cannot be asserted that exact data do not exist in any official channel.
In 2025, the average annual wage of employed persons in scientific research and technical services in urban non-private units in mainland China was {{fact:cn-wage-nonprivate}}.

In 2025, the average annual wage of employed persons in scientific research and technical services in urban private units in mainland China was {{fact:cn-wage-private}}; non-private and private are two different statistical scopes, cannot be mixed, and exclude self-employed individuals and freelancers.

Actual pay for this occupation also depends on the city, the type of employer (semiconductor and materials manufacturing, research institutes, testing institutions), shift patterns and cleanroom allowances, and experience and skill level, and should be verified against public job postings and contracts.
The wage shown on the United States O*NET page is {{fact:us-wage}}, under the Industrial Engineering Technologists and Technicians parent occupation scope, and is not the figure for 17-3026.01 alone.
This wage statistic cannot be interpreted as starting pay, a personal quote, or an income promise; percentiles are only statistical positions and do not represent experience or job level.

When comparing United States positions, also verify the state, industry (manufacturing, professional and technical services), shifts, overtime and cleanroom allowances, benefits, and work authorization conditions.
The O*NET page already states that wages and employment use the parent occupation scope, and this page preserves that proxy boundary and does not disguise it as a standalone median.
A job offer should be verified against employer recruitment information and local rules; official statistics only describe the employed population they cover.
United States figures cannot be directly converted into or extrapolated as individual income in mainland China.

risks.mitigation: Editorial suggestion: first verify the target site's risk assessment and approved operating procedures, and confirm protective equipment, equipment isolation, and shutdown processes; stop and report when something is abnormal, and do not determine statutory control requirements from the O*NET task list alone.
risks.scenario: Operational risks when operating nanofabrication, coating, or high-pressure equipment; O*NET shows that 35% are exposed to hazardous conditions daily, 60% wear common protective equipment daily, and 15% consider the consequences of error extremely serious
risks.title: Equipment operation and personal safety

risks.affected_roles: Technicians responsible for sample preparation, clean operation, and measurement
risks.consequence: May make measurement data lose comparability and affect batch-wide result judgments
risks.mitigation: Isolate suspicious samples per cleanliness requirements and record the conditions; editorial suggestion: have occupational hygiene personnel assess the material, process, exposure duration, and existing engineering controls before determining on-site protection, and do not equate clean operation with health exposure control.
risks.scenario: Sample contamination affects measurement; processes involving nanomaterials may also create occupational exposure through inhalation, ingestion, or skin contact, and the specific pathway varies with material and operation.
risks.title: Sample contamination and data distortion risk

risks.affected_roles: Technicians who handle undisclosed process parameters and client sample data
risks.consequence: May cause intellectual property loss and compliance disputes
risks.mitigation: Editorial suggestion: handle undisclosed processes and client data only through authorized channels and keep records, and verify contractual confidentiality obligations and applicable law; whether export control applies must be judged by the specific technology, entity, and jurisdiction.
risks.scenario: Entering undisclosed process parameters, formulations, or client data into unauthorized external tools or services
risks.title: Process parameter leakage risk

risks.affected_roles: Technicians working outside trained and authorized boundaries
risks.consequence: May cause equipment damage, safety incidents, and responsibility disputes
risks.mitigation: Verify the training and authorization list, and stop and hand it to authorized personnel when out of scope
risks.scenario: Operating equipment, handling anomalies, or changing process parameters without training or authorization
risks.title: Risk of operating beyond authorization

risks.affected_roles: Technicians responsible for calibration, maintenance, and consumable replacement
risks.consequence: May accumulate measurement deviations and affect result reliability
risks.mitigation: Calibrate and replace consumables per the maintenance plan, and keep maintenance records and acceptance conclusions
risks.scenario: Not calibrating or replacing consumables per plan, with incomplete maintenance records
risks.title: Improper equipment maintenance risk

risks.affected_roles: Technicians working shifts and repetitive operations on the manufacturing floor
risks.consequence: May cause fatigue, reduced attention, and more operating errors
risks.mitigation: Rotate shifts and rest per the schedule, follow operating duration and health and safety rules, and give feedback to supervisors
risks.scenario: O*NET shows that 35% work more than 40 hours per week, some positions use shift systems, and repetitive operation time is long
risks.title: Shift and repetitive work load

questions.answer: Keep equipment parameter records, measurement data, calibration and maintenance records, abnormal shutdown and handling records, and supervisor feedback.
questions.question: How do you accumulate reviewable professional evidence?

questions.answer: Complete one operation and recording exercise using public manuals or simulated data, write the safety preconditions, record fields, and abnormal shutdown conditions, and then ask on-site staff for feedback.
questions.question: What kind of low-cost trial is best to start with for verification?

signals.body: You will operate equipment step by step per work instructions, record parameters faithfully, accept repeated measurement and cleaning and maintenance, and proactively shut down and report when readings deviate or safety risks appear.
signals.label: Fit signals

signals.body: If you find it hard to follow safety and cleanliness procedures over the long term, avoid record review, cannot adapt to shift schedules, or expect to do only design and not on-site execution, this occupation will be very draining.
signals.label: Signals that call for caution

signals.body: Complete one operation recording exercise using public equipment manuals or simulated data: write the operating steps, safety preconditions, record fields, calibration requirements, and two abnormal shutdown conditions, and then ask an experienced technician to give feedback against on-site standards.
signals.label: Low-cost trial

components.work_context_block: Work context (O*NET work context survey, United States respondent percentages): 90% work indoors in a controlled environment every day, 100% use email daily, and 65% hold face-to-face discussions daily; 60% consider precision or high accuracy extremely important; 65% have a 40-hour work week and 35% work more than 40 hours, and 80% have a regular work schedule; about 80% report a great deal or some freedom in tasks and decisions; 15% consider the consequences of error extremely serious and 30% carry very high responsibility for the health and safety of others; 60% wear common protective equipment daily, 35% are exposed to hazardous conditions daily, and 50% consider the work only slightly automated. Job Zone 4 is an occupation group preparation level, and its general training period cannot be treated as a uniform duration for this occupation; industry shares must be verified separately against the current table period and the parent occupation scope.

description.text: Nanotechnology engineering technologists and technicians (O*NET 17-3026.01) implement production processes under the supervision of nanotechnology engineering staff, operating commercial-scale equipment to produce and test nanoscale materials and devices, and use advanced microscopy equipment to manipulate nanoscale objects.
